text:
Predicates:
SpillsFoodOnClothing(x) ::: x spills a lot of food on their clothing.
NotablyTidy(x) ::: x is notably tidy.
ClumsyFoodie(x) ::: x is a clumsy foodie.
GoesOutFrequent(x) ::: x goes out frequently to find new food restaurants.
Cleanly(x) ::: x is cleanly.
ValuatesOrderAndSpotlessness(x) ::: x values order and spotlessness.
FamilyPrioritizesOrderAndSpotlessness(x) ::: x's family prioritizes order and spotlessness.
Peter(x) ::: x is Peter.
Family(x, y) ::: x's family prioritizes y.

Premises:
∀x (SpillsFoodOnClothing(x) → ¬NotablyTidy(x)) ::: If people spill a lot of food on their clothing, then they are not notably tidy.
∀x (GoesOutFrequent(x) ∧ ClumsyFoodie(x) → SpillsFoodOnClothing(x)) ::: All clumsy foodies who go out frequently are people who spill a lot of food on their clothing.
∀x (Cleanly(x) → NotablyTidy(x)) ::: If people are cleanly, then they are notably tidy.
∀x (ValuatesOrderAndSpotlessness(x) → Cleanly(x)) ::: If people value order and spotlessness, then they are cleanly.
∀x (Family(x, y) ∧ PrioritizesOrderAndSpotlessness(y) → ValuatesOrderAndSpotlessness(x)) ::: All people whose families prioritize order and spotlessness value order and spotlessness.
Peter(x) ∧ (SpillsFoodOnClothing(x) ∧ Cleanly(x)) ∨ (¬SpillsFoodOnClothing(x) ∧ ¬Cleanly(x)) ::: Peter is either a person who spills a lot of food on his clothing and is cleanly, or a person who does not spill a lot of food and is not cleanly.

Conclusion:
(ClumsyFoodie(x) ∧ GoesOutFrequent(x)) ∨ (FamilyPrioritizesOrderAndSpotlessness(y) ∧ Family(x, y)) ::: Peter is either a clumsy foodie who goes out frequently to find new food restaurants to try or someone whose family prioritizes order and spotlessness.
